newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs put little faith in austerity plan, cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Czechs put little faith in austerity plan, cabinet.

text.p: Nearly half the Czech electorate thinks Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his centre-right cabinet should resign after admitting that major policy mistakes led to a currency crisis, a survey released on Monday showed.
Only about one in five think the government's new austerity plan to stabilise the economy will succeed.

"Ordinary people will ask...whether the government realised there were such serious problems only under the pressure of an intensifying crisis or whether it had known about the problems for a long time but chose to ignore them," political scientist Jiri Pehe said.

But the poll for the daily Mlada Fronta Dnes newspaper by the private agency Factum also highlighted the paradox that few Czechs can see anybody other than the monetarist economist Klaus, in power since 1992, as prime minister.

Klaus has vowed to fight his critics and implement the ruling coalition's programme aimed at restoring confidence in the Czech crown which has lost more than 15 percent of its value against major currencies since February.
The poll, taken two days after Klaus introduced the programme on May 28, indicates that the government faces a huge battle to restore public confidence.

Only 22.5 percent of 1,028 adults surveyed said the three-party coalition could correct the economy with its planned budget cuts, public sector wage freezes, and steps to slow domestic demand which has created huge trade deficits.

The percentage of Czechs thinking the entire government should step down rose to 46.3 percent on May 30 from 14.9 percent in a similar poll taken on May 18-19 before a shakeup of the cabinet was promised.
Klaus offered steps last Wednesday to solve a balance of payments problem which sparked a sharp fall in the crown over the past two weeks and forced the central bank to float the currency.

Along with the plan -- which accompanied a shuffle in the cabinet including replacing Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik with Education Minister Ivan Pilip -- the normally confident Klaus took the surprising step of admitting that mistakes were made.

Political analysts said the plan would be a tough sell to Czechs who have already lost faith in a government after being told by Klaus before elections last June that their wages could double in the next four years under his leadership.
"(The Klaus programme) will probably fail to generate the kind of credibility this government needs to work productively and survive," said Pehe.

Despite the distrust in the government, the Factum poll showed that 21.9 percent of Czechs think Klaus should still be premier, compared with 11.9 percent saying it should be Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman.
A total of 27.4 percent said they did not know who should be prime minister.
On Friday, Klaus ruled out resigning and said he would fight to get his programme approved in the lower house of parliament where the ruling coalition holds 100 of the 200 seats.

On Saturday, Klaus said he would seek a vote of confidence in the government -- probably on June 10 or 11 -- before the opposition Social Democrats could move a vote of no-confidence which they have threatened.
